title: A job application, from draft to outcome
summary: The eight statuses an application record can hold, the pipeline the Career workspace presents, and the three that close it. Both the enum and the direction of travel are enforced now; which of the forward moves an operator takes is theirs to choose.
note: Read the arrows as the route an application usually takes, not as the whole of what the machine admits. An application is an ordinary graph node: its status is a required enum on `applicationProps` (packages/core/src/schema/node-props.ts:193), and the machine over it is `APPLICATION_STATUS_FLOW` and `canTransition` (packages/core/src/schema/application.ts:66). The rule is forward-permissive: from any open stage a record may move to any LATER open stage, or close on any of the three outcomes. Not every role has a recruiter screen, so `applied` to `interview` has to be recordable, and a machine that refused it would be refusing something that happened. What it refuses is the pair of moves that can only be a mistake: walking backwards down the pipeline, and reopening a record that already carries an outcome. A refusal names both ends of the move and the way out (packages/core/src/schema/application.ts:102) rather than saying the value was invalid, which would send an operator looking for a typo in a word they spelled correctly. Every writer runs it. `POST /applications`, `PATCH /applications/:id` and `POST /applications/:id/status` share one guard with the generic node patch (apps/api/src/routes/v1/nodes.ts:233), because the generic patch is the request the application form itself sends and a guard it skipped would be a guard nothing in the product obeyed. Correcting a status is a different act and has a different door. A move says the application reached a new stage; a correction says the recorded status was never true, so it skips the machine and is written with a `correction` provenance, which is what lets the history afterwards tell a record that moved from a record whose last entry had simply been wrong. Without it the guard would trap an operator who mis-clicked `rejected`, and a guard that makes true data unfixable is worse than no guard. Three things deliberately pass the guard: props that never mention a status, a status resubmitted as itself (editing a deadline resends the whole record), and a stored status the enum cannot read, which `statusOf` falls back to `draft` (apps/api/src/routes/v1/applications.ts:67) so one pre-schema record cannot become one nobody may edit. Creation is unguarded on purpose: an application entered after the fact may already have been rejected, and insisting every record begin at `draft` would refuse a fact. Two notes on scope. The eight statuses and the pipeline ordering are declared once, in core (packages/core/src/schema/application.ts:20), and the props schema, the form select, the OpenAPI document and the workspace's columns all read that one list. And a job posting carries its own separate status vocabulary, watching, interested, applied, closed, passed (packages/core/src/schema/node-props.ts:185), which this machine does not govern.

states.label: Draft
states.note: The record exists but nothing has been sent. Also the fallback the API reads for a record whose stored status it cannot parse (apps/api/src/routes/v1/applications.ts:67), so a pre-schema bundle stays readable instead of breaking the whole workspace.

states.label: Applied
states.note: Submitted. `applied_on` is a separate optional date field, not derived from the status, so the two can disagree.

states.label: Screening
states.note: Recruiter or resume screen. Counted as active: it is not in `CLOSED_STATUSES`.

states.label: Interview
states.note: Interview rounds are separate `interview` nodes joined by `INTERVIEW_FOR` edges, each with its own outcome enum — scheduled, passed, failed, pending, cancelled (packages/core/src/schema/node-props.ts:228). A failed round does not move the application; a person does.

states.label: Offer
states.note: An offer is on the table. Still open — the decision has not been recorded.

states.label: Accepted
states.note: Closed. Counted out of `active` and out of `needs_attention`, so an overdue next step on an accepted application stops nagging.

states.label: Rejected
states.note: Closed by the other side. Sorted below every open application in the list.

states.label: Withdrawn
states.note: Closed by you. The enum does not distinguish withdrawing before a reply from withdrawing after an offer.

transitions.label: Submit the application
transitions.note: Set on the record through the application form's status select; `applied_on` and `next_step_date` are filled in the same dialog.

transitions.label: They replied and a screen is scheduled
Straight to interviews, with no screen
transitions.note: Drawn because it is the case that forced the machine to be forward-permissive rather than step-by-step. Every other forward skip is admitted too and left undrawn: twenty-five arrows would render as a mesh and say less than this sentence does.

transitions.label: Passed the screen; interview rounds begin
Another round
transitions.note: Nothing in the status changes between rounds. The round is a new `interview` node joined by an `INTERVIEW_FOR` edge; the dossier lists them in stage order and surfaces the next one whose outcome is not cancelled, passed or failed.

transitions.label: Accept the offer
transitions.note: The only transition into `accepted` the interface's own stage ordering suggests.

transitions.label: Rejected without a screen
transitions.note: `rejected` is one of the three statuses the API treats as closed, which is what removes it from the active count and the attention count.

transitions.label: Offer pulled
transitions.note: The enum has no separate value for a rescinded offer; `rejected` absorbs it.

transitions.label: Decline the offer
transitions.note: Declining and withdrawing share one value, so the list cannot tell an offer you turned down from an application you dropped.
